doc.title: Von Freeman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
title: Embouchure, double lip and Link mouthpieces
summary: They discuss double-lip playing and Dyett's reaction, metal mouthpieces and Freeman's fifty-year-old Link.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: So, who knows? It may be. There seemed to be a similarity. They had that really tight thing, smile, and not everybody – a whole lot of cats don’t have that kind of embouchure.

No. Well, they can’t get the dexterity that they want with it, because you know, it’s an old saying, that in order to get the dexterity, you got to have your mouth so that the reed can vibrate freely. So that – that’s a myth. But the embouchure that really puzzled me was Coltrane, and Johnny Hodges. It was a long time before I realized that they were playing double lip. Because, see, when I first went to high school, that’s the first thing that Captain Walter Dyett told me. He says, “You’re playing double lip?” I say, “Well, that’s the way I play.” He said, “Oh, you won’t play that way long.” I didn’t know what he meant, because he put me right into marching band with that bass saxophone.
That stopped all that.

Oh man. I stepped into a hole one day, and I bit through up here. He said, “I noticed you’re not” – about two months later, he said, “I noticed you’re not playing double lip anymore,” because when he wanted to be cynical, that’s the way he talked. “Oh, you’re not playing double lip.” I said, “No sir.” But the . . .
This guy Alvin Batiste, you know him?
Yeah.
Down in Louisiana.
Yeah, the clarinet player.
Yeah, he teaches those cats double lip. So Donald Harrison and Branford Marsalis and all those cats.

Oh yeah. You get a beautiful sound. You really do, much because your teeth are not on the mouthpiece. Because my teeth used to be beautiful. I was fooling around. The minute I started blowing with these Link mouthpieces . . .
Metal mouthpieces will do it.
Teeth divided.
Teeth divided. Yeah, they’ll do it to you.
A lot of cats, their mouth is round like this, because those are hard mouthpieces.
I always played hard rubber. I never played metal. I mean, I tried to play metal, but I . . .
See, that – you just have to – it’s an acquired taste.
It’s one of those things that certain cats were playing Links, and because of that, everybody – they wanted to be like them, get that sound.
Right.
So there was a period when Links were real popular.
They’re not that popular anymore.
Plus they don’t make them the same way. It’s not the same.

No, no, no, because my mouthpiece like is – what? – 50-something years old. Everybody said, man, you’re still playing that mouthpiece? I say, I can’t find a new Link that sounds like anything. I’ve almost bitten through this one.
